śūdras
------------------------------------------
See VARṆA and VARṆĀŚRAMADHARMA.

Sudāma
------------------------------------------
Sudāma (or Śrīdāma) as a poor ब्राह्मण boy, was a classmate and an intimate friend of कृष्ण in the गुरुकुल (forest academy) of the sage सान्दीपनि. Since he used to wear bad and worn out clothes, he was also called कुचेल.
After मर्रिअगे and with a big family he used to suffer much due to poverty. At the insistence of his wife, he went to द्वारका to see कृष्ण and beg some wealth from him. He had carried with him some flattened rice for कृष्ण as an offering. When Kṛṣna ate a handful of the same, his होउसे at his village was transformed into a palatial mansion with plenty of wealth!
He is cited as an example of sakhya-भक्ति (devotion to God as a friend) (vide Bhāgavata 10.80 and 81).

Sudāsa
------------------------------------------
Sudāsa—the son of दिवोदास and a descendent of Pijavana—was a king of the Bhārata race. In the दाशराज्ञ episode of the Ṛgveda (7.33.3, 5; 7.83.8) he is said to have defeated the combined armies of the ten kings of races like the Pakthas, the Bhalānas, the Vaṣānins and others. His chief priest was वसिष्ठ whereas the latter kings were guided by विश्वामित्र.
The अश्विन्स् gave him Sudevī as his queen. इन्द्र is said to have helped him in all his invasions.
He was a great king known for his generous gifts.

Sudarśanasūri
(A.

-1275)
------------------------------------------
He was the son of Digvijayabhaṭṭa and the grandson of Vedavyāsabhaṭṭa who himself was the second son of कूरेश, the famous disciple of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137).
He was the author of the now famous Śrutaprakāśikā, a detailed gloss on the Śrībhāṣya of Rāmānuja.
Vedānta Deśika (A.

-1369) was his younger contemporary, who tactfully managed to save सुदर्शनसूरि’s book as also his two sons during the Muslim invasion of South India.
The other works of सुदर्शनसूरि are: Śrutapradīpikā, Tātparyadīpikā, Śaraṇāgatigadyabhāṣya, a commentary on the Subālopaniṣad, Sandhyāvandana-bhāṣya and Kṣamāṣoḍaśī.

Śuddhādvaita
(‘the pure advaita’)
------------------------------------------
The system of philosophy of Vallabhā-cārya or वल्लभ (A.

-1531) is known as शुद्धाद्वैत.
Vallabha does not accept शङ्कर’s (A.

-820) advaita as sufficiently non-dualistic since he also accepts māyā, a principle of इल्लुसिओन्, thereby negating non-dualism!
According to वल्लभ, māyā is a real power of ब्रह्मन्, the Saccidānanda, inherent in him. Hence, since there is no second reality different from or outside ब्रह्मन्, his philosophy should be called Śuddhādvaita—is his claim.
See also VALLABHA.

śuddhamāyā
(‘pure māyā’)
------------------------------------------
In the Siddha system of medicine शुद्धमाया is pure matter and अशुद्ध-माया is impure matter. The latter is corruptible whereas the former is always incorruptible.
When by a special method, the aśuddhamāyā is purified and brought into the line of शुद्धमाया, there will be no bodily death. The method, however, has to be learnt from the expert सिद्धस्.
In काश्मीर् शैविस्म्, शुद्धमाया is the intrinsic power of शिव to create the world, sustain it and withdraw it—like the burning power of fire—in its purest form.
When it manifests itself in the form of the five कञ्चुकस् (or sheaths) and apparently binds शिव it becomes aśuddhamāyā or impure māyā.
See ‘Kāśmīr शैविस्म्’ under ŚAIVISM.

Sudarśana
(‘that which has a nice appearance’)
------------------------------------------
Sudarśana is the name of the चक्र or discus of Lord विष्णु. In his इन्चर्नतिओन् as कृष्ण he used this weapon quite often.
According to certain Śaiva पुराणस्, शिव is said to have gifted it to विष्णु who had worshipped him with great devotion at काशी.
In इचोनोग्रफ्य् सुदर्शन is treated as āyudhapuruṣa (personified deity of the weapon) and also as an independent deity. He is shown as a figure similar to विष्णु, but with six arms (or hands). Behind him there is a hexagonal frame enclosed in a flaming circle.

śuddhi
(‘purification’)
------------------------------------------
Śuddhi or purification—which is more ceremonial than physical—is a very vast subject. It covers such areas as अशौच (impurity that accrues to a person due to the birth or the death of a near relative) (See AŚAUCA for details.), purification of a person after contact with an impure object or on certain occurrences, and purification of ड़ोओद्, vessels, ponds and other things after they are polluted.
The literature on शुद्धि is very extensive.
Śuddhi has been categorised in several ways; for instance: bāhya (external, like bath) and āntara (internal, like purity of emotions). According to another classification, शुद्धि comprises purity of body, of speech, of मिन्द् and of financial dealings. A third one states शुद्धि consists in avoiding forbidden ड़ोओद्, in associating only with sinless persons and in firmly abiding by one’s स्वधर्म (prescribed duties).
However, all dharmaśāstra treatises stress the importance of mental purity.
It is interesting to note that the Āpastamba Śrautasūtras (2.12) declares that the performer of the Pavitreṣṭi (and two more similar iṣṭis or sacrifices) purifies himself and ten generations of his family.
Various expiatory rites (prāyaścittas) also purify a person who might have committed sins or evil deeds, knowingly or unknowingly.
The word शुद्धि has also been used for the process of reconversion to हिन्दुइस्म्. See PARĀVARTANA for details.
